patient.name: Grace Mensah
patient.complaint: Sharp central chest pain for 2 days, worse lying flat and better sitting forward
background: Systemic lupus erythematosus for 6 years, on hydroxychloroquine
Flu-like illness with fever last week
Lives in Lewisham, works as a nursery manager
No known drug allergies; no history of peptic ulcer

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with positional chest pain and a rub (pericarditis), Beck's triad after surgery or trauma (tamponade), or raised JVP, ascites and a knock (constrictive).

points: Grace, 32, has **SLE**; flu-like illness last week.
Sharp **retrosternal** pain, worse **lying flat**, breathing in and coughing.
Scratchy, high-pitched sound at the left sternal edge.

steps.lead: Grace's pericardium is inflamed. Her recent viral illness (and her **SLE**) are both recognised causes.
Grace has the classic triad of **acute pericarditis**: positional pleuritic pain, flu-like prodrome and a **friction rub**.

steps.q: Grace's pain is sharp, worse lying flat and relieved by sitting forward. Which diagnosis fits best?
steps.r: Positional pain eased by **sitting forward** with a **rub** is pericarditis. ACS pain is crushing; dissection tears to the back.

steps.title: Chest pain that can mimic pericarditis
head: Feature
Pericarditis
STEMI
PE

points: Day 3: Grace becomes breathless and light-headed.
JVP raised to the earlobe; heart sounds now **muffled**.
Systolic BP falls by 22 mmHg when she breathes in.

steps.lead: Grace now has **Beck's triad** (raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds) and **pulsus paradoxus**: cardiac tamponade.

visual.title: Grace's inspiratory fall in systolic BP
visual.label: Grace 22 mmHg
visual.caption: A fall of **more than 15 mmHg** on inspiration is pulsus paradoxus.

steps.lead: Grace's **SLE** is a recognised risk factor for tamponade, alongside malignancy, recent cardiac surgery, trauma and anticoagulation.
Grace's illness is acute. If inflammation became chronic and fibrotic, she could develop **constrictive pericarditis** instead.

steps.text: Hypotension + raised JVP has three classic causes: **tamponade**, tension pneumothorax and massive PE. Muffled heart sounds and equal breath sounds point to tamponade.

investigation.exam: Expect ECG questions (PR depression is most specific; widespread saddle ST elevation) and echo as the test that confirms effusion or tamponade.

steps.q: Grace arrives with positional chest pain. Which test confirms pericarditis?
steps.r: The **ECG** is the gold standard for pericarditis. Echo is the gold standard for **effusion and tamponade**.

visual.title: Grace's ECG on arrival
visual.caption: Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation, not in one coronary territory. Look for **PR depression**, the most specific sign.

steps.lead: Grace's ECG shows **PR depression** and widespread saddle ST elevation. Her troponin is mildly up and CRP raised; she still needs a TTE.

steps.title: Grace's bloods
steps.text: A mildly raised troponin reflects myopericardial inflammation. Normal urea rules out uraemic pericarditis.

steps.lead: Grace's **ECG** confirmed pericarditis. When she deteriorates, **echo** is what confirms the effusion and tamponade.

points: Day 3 bedside echo: large circumferential **pericardial effusion**.
ECG: small QRS complexes that alternate in height beat to beat.

steps.lead: Grace's tamponade is diagnosed on **echo**. Her CXR has a globular heart and her ECG shows **electrical alternans**.

visual.title: Grace's chest X-ray, day 3
visual.caption: Enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette with clear lungs: the **'water bottle' sign** of a large effusion.

steps.text: Do not label widespread ST elevation as a STEMI. A STEMI follows **one coronary territory** with reciprocal depression; pericarditis is **diffuse** with PR depression.

management.exam: Expect NSAID plus colchicine for acute pericarditis, colchicine alone with peptic ulcer, and urgent sub-xiphoid pericardiocentesis for tamponade.

points: Started **ibuprofen** plus **colchicine**, with a PPI and rest.

steps.lead: Grace gets the first-line regimen: **NSAID plus colchicine** with rest. With a peptic ulcer, she would get colchicine alone.

steps.q: If Grace had an active peptic ulcer, what would replace ibuprofen plus colchicine?
steps.r: NSAIDs are avoided in **peptic ulcer disease**, so **colchicine alone** is the second-line option.

steps.lead: On day 3 Grace is in tamponade: she needs **urgent pericardiocentesis**, sub-xiphoid and ultrasound-guided.

steps.title: Cardiac tamponade
nodes: Bedside echo confirms effusion with RV diastolic collapse
Needle just left of xiphoid, aimed at the left shoulder
steps.caption: Sub-xiphoid has the lowest pneumothorax risk when done blind.

visual.title: Grace before and after drainage
visual.caption: Removing 450 mL of fluid restores filling: BP rises and the heart rate settles at once.

steps.lead: After drainage, a small residual effusion is just **monitored**. Constriction would need **diuretics** and possibly **pericardiectomy**.
Grace's care tracks the key definitions: **Beck's triad**, **pulsus paradoxus** over 15 mmHg, and **NSAID + colchicine** first line.

steps.text: Diuretics or GTN in tamponade drop preload and can precipitate arrest. The fix is **drainage**, not offloading.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanisms: why the pain is positional, why tamponade causes shock and pulsus paradoxus, and why electrical alternans occurs.

steps.lead: Grace's inflamed pericardial layers rub and irritate pain fibres, so her pain changes with **position** and **breathing**.
Grace's fluid built up **faster than the pericardium could stretch**, so pressure rose until it matched the filling pressures.

steps.title: From effusion to tamponade
nodes: Fluid collects in the pericardial sac
Intrapericardial pressure rises to equal chamber pressure
Right heart cannot fill in diastole
Stroke volume and BP fall: shock

steps.q: Why did Grace's systolic BP fall on inspiration?
o: Inspiration fills the RV, which bulges the septum into the LV
steps.r: In a fixed-volume sac, extra RV filling on inspiration pushes the **septum** into the LV, cutting LV output: **pulsus paradoxus**.

steps.lead: Constrictive pericarditis is the same 'restricted filling' problem but from a **rigid fibrotic shell**, developing slowly.
Grace's small, alternating QRS complexes came from her heart **swinging** in the fluid, changing its electrical axis each beat.

steps.text: Small volume, fast = tamponade (e.g. 150 mL of blood after surgery). Large volume, slow = may be tolerated because the pericardium stretches.

mcq.q: What is the most important cause of acute pericarditis?
mcq.r: **Viral** (Coxsackie, echovirus, EBV, CMV, HIV, VZV) or idiopathic.

mcq.q: What are the components of Beck's triad?
o: Raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds
mcq.r: **Raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds**: tamponade.

o: Systolic BP fall >15 mmHg on inspiration
mcq.r: A drop in systolic BP of **more than 15 mmHg** on inspiration.
An early diastolic **pericardial knock**, with raised JVP and ascites.
Autoimmune pericarditis **weeks after MI**; can lead to constriction.

mcq.q: What is the most specific ECG finding in acute pericarditis?
mcq.r: **PR depression** is the most specific; saddle ST elevation is common.

mcq.q: What CXR sign suggests a large pericardial effusion?

o: Heart swinging in a large effusion
mcq.r: The heart **swings** in the fluid, changing its axis beat to beat.

prompts.q: What are the symptoms and signs of acute pericarditis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the position of the patient gives it away.

points.p: Worse lying flat, inspiring or coughing; relieved sitting forward

points.why: Scratchy, at the left sternal edge.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the background in the stem names the cause.

points.p: Viral: Coxsackie, echovirus, EBV, CMV, HIV, VZV; or idiopathic

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: Beck's triad plus pulsus paradoxus.

points.p: Beck's triad: raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds
Pulsus paradoxus: systolic drop >15 mmHg on inspiration
Kussmaul's sign and absent Y descent

prompts.q: What are the risk factors for tamponade?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: what put fluid or blood in the sac?

points.why: Fatigue, arthralgia, malar rash, oral ulcers.

points.p: Recent cardiac surgery or pacemaker; trauma

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: right heart failure with a knock.

points.p: Rigid thickened pericardium limiting diastolic filling
Raised JVP, positive hepatojugular reflux, ascites, right HF signs

prompts.q: Which tests confirm pericarditis and tamponade, and what do they show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ECG for pericarditis, echo for fluid.

points.p: ECG is the gold standard for pericarditis
points.why: Every case also gets a TTE.
Learn this as the most specific.

points.p: Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation and Spodick's sign
Echo is the gold standard for effusion and tamponade

prompts.q: What do CXR and ECG show with a large effusion?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: water bottle and alternans.

points.p: ECG: electrical alternans with small QRS complexes

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: check for peptic ulcer before an NSAID.

points.p: Avoid NSAIDs in peptic ulcer disease: colchicine monotherapy

prompts.q: How is tamponade managed, and what about special causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: drain it, and know the exceptions.

points.why: Do not delay for imaging if peri-arrest.
Aim to the left shoulder; lowest pneumothorax risk.

prompts.q: Why does an effusion cause tamponade and pulsus paradoxus?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: speed of accumulation matters.

points.p: Fluid accumulates faster than the pericardium can stretch
points.why: Small fast bleeds can be lethal.

points.p: Intrapericardial pressure equals or exceeds chamber pressure

prompts.q: Why is the pain positional, and why does electrical alternans occur?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: link the anatomy to the sign.

points.p: Inflamed visceral and parietal layers irritate pain fibres
Alternans: the heart swings in a large effusion, changing axis beat to beat
Constriction: fibrosis and calcification form a rigid shell over time

glossary.Pericardium: The fibrous two-layered sac around the heart.
glossary.Pericardial effusion: Fluid collecting in the pericardial sac.
glossary.Cardiac tamponade: Fluid in the pericardium compressing the heart so it cannot fill; a medical emergency.
glossary.Tamponade: Compression of the heart by pericardial fluid.
glossary.Constrictive pericarditis: A thick, rigid pericardium that limits diastolic filling, developing over months to years.
glossary.Friction rub: Scratchy sound heard as inflamed pericardial layers rub together.
glossary.Pericardial friction rub: Scratchy, high-pitched sound from inflamed pericardial layers rubbing together.
glossary.Beck's triad: Raised JVP, hypotension and muffled heart sounds in cardiac tamponade.
glossary.Pulsus paradoxus: A fall in systolic BP of more than 15 mmHg on inspiration.
glossary.Kussmaul's sign: A paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration.
glossary.JVP: Jugular venous pressure: height of the venous pulsation in the neck, reflecting right atrial pressure.
glossary.Y descent: The fall in the JVP waveform as the tricuspid valve opens; absent in tamponade.
glossary.Pericardial knock: An early diastolic sound in constrictive pericarditis as filling stops abruptly.
glossary.Hepatojugular reflux: A sustained rise in JVP when pressing on the liver.
glossary.PR depression: Depression of the PR segment on ECG; the most specific sign of pericarditis.
glossary.Saddle-shaped ST elevation: Concave ST elevation across many leads, typical of pericarditis.
glossary.Spodick's sign: A downsloping TP segment on the ECG in acute pericarditis.
glossary.Electrical alternans: QRS height alternating beat to beat as the heart swings in a large effusion.
glossary.Water bottle sign: A large, globular heart shadow on chest X-ray from a big pericardial effusion.
glossary.Echocardiography: Ultrasound of the heart; confirms effusion and tamponade.
glossary.TTE: Transthoracic echocardiography: heart ultrasound through the chest wall.
glossary.Pericardiocentesis: Draining pericardial fluid with a needle, ideally sub-xiphoid under ultrasound.
glossary.Sub-xiphoid: Just below the xiphisternum; the preferred route for pericardiocentesis.
glossary.Pericardiectomy: Surgical removal of the pericardium for constrictive pericarditis.
glossary.Balloon pericardiotomy: A balloon catheter makes a window in the pericardium, used for malignant effusions.
glossary.Colchicine: Anti-inflammatory drug that reduces pericarditis symptoms and recurrence.
glossary.NSAID: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as ibuprofen or naproxen.
glossary.Dressler's syndrome: Autoimmune pericarditis occurring weeks after a myocardial infarction.
glossary.Uraemic pericarditis: Pericarditis caused by high urea in kidney failure; treated with dialysis.
glossary.SLE: Systemic lupus erythematosus: autoimmune disease that can cause serositis, including pericarditis.
glossary.Behçet's syndrome: Vasculitis with mouth and genital ulcers; a cause of pericarditis.
glossary.Coxsackie: An enterovirus that commonly causes viral pericarditis and myocarditis.
glossary.Haemopericardium: Blood in the pericardial sac, e.g. after trauma or cardiac surgery.
glossary.HFpEF: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: the ventricle pumps but fills poorly.
glossary.Muffled heart sounds: Quiet heart sounds because fluid around the heart dampens them.

technique.stem: A 67 year old man with lung cancer has 3 weeks of increasing breathlessness and chest discomfort. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and there is no fall in systolic BP on inspiration. His JVP is raised and his heart sounds are quiet. His lungs are clear. Chest X-ray shows an enlarged globular heart.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: decide effusion vs tamponade vs constriction.

clues: no fall in systolic BP on inspiration
steps.x: Malignancy, progressive breathlessness, raised JVP, muffled sounds, water bottle heart, but **normal BP** and no pulsus paradoxus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **pericardial effusion** that has not yet caused tamponade.

elim: Tamponade needs hypotension and pulsus paradoxus; his BP is normal.
Constriction is chronic with a knock and ascites.
Dilated cardiomyopathy gives a displaced apex, S3 and pulmonary oedema.
A pleural effusion is in the chest, not the cardiac silhouette; lungs are clear.

steps.x: **D. Pericardial effusion.** Add hypotension and it becomes tamponade.

technique.stem: A 23 year old man has 2 days of sharp central chest pain that is worse lying down and when he breathes in, and better leaning forward. He had a sore throat last week. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg. A scratchy sound is heard at the left sternal edge.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation for suspected pericarditis.
Positional pleuritic pain, viral prodrome, friction rub: acute pericarditis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **12-lead ECG**: the gold standard test for pericarditis (PR depression, saddle ST elevation).

elim: CXR is usually normal unless there is a big effusion.
CTPA is for PE; the pain is positional, not sudden with hypoxia.
D-dimer is for low-probability PE.
An exercise test in acute inflammation is unsafe and unhelpful.

steps.x: **A. ECG.** Then TTE in every suspected pericarditis.

technique.stem: A 59 year old man is 2 hours after coronary artery bypass surgery. He becomes hypotensive with a raised JVP and quiet heart sounds. His pulse rate is 134 bpm, BP 76/50 mmHg. Bedside echo shows a pericardial collection with right ventricular diastolic collapse. Chest drain output has suddenly stopped.
technique.q: Which is the preferred approach to drain the fluid if done blind?

steps.x: The question asks for the approach for pericardiocentesis.

clues: 2 hours after coronary artery bypass surgery
raised JVP and quiet heart sounds
steps.x: Beck's triad after cardiac surgery with echo collapse: tamponade.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sub-xiphoid** pericardiocentesis, ideally under ultrasound guidance.

elim: Apical carries a higher risk of pneumothorax and ventricular puncture.
Parasternal risks pneumothorax and the internal mammary artery.
Right parasternal is not a standard approach.
Thoracoscopy is not an emergency drainage route in shock.

steps.x: **D. Sub-xiphoid**: needle left of the xiphoid, aim at the left shoulder.

technique.stem: A 40 year old woman is stabbed in the chest. Within 20 minutes she is hypotensive with distended neck veins and quiet heart sounds. Pericardiocentesis removes only 120 mL of blood and her BP rises from 70/40 to 110/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason such a small volume caused shock?
o: Blood is more viscous than serous fluid
Fluid accumulated faster than the pericardium could stretch

steps.x: Mechanism: why did a small, fast bleed cause tamponade?
Rapid bleed, small volume, instant improvement on drainage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The pericardium **cannot stretch quickly**, so pressure rises sharply and blocks filling.

elim: Viscosity does not determine pericardial pressure.
Contractility was fine; she improved instantly on drainage.
The problem is filling, not coronary flow.
120 mL of blood loss would not cause shock by itself.

steps.x: **B.** Speed, not volume, causes tamponade.

practice.stem: A 26 year old man has 3 days of sharp central chest pain that is worse when lying flat and better sitting forward. He had a flu-like illness last week. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 126/74 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. A scratchy sound is heard at the left sternal edge. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Positional chest pain eased by sitting forward, a friction rub, a viral prodrome and widespread saddle ST elevation is acute pericarditis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of chest pain: use the position and the ECG.
Positional pain + rub + viral prodrome + **widespread** ST elevation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute pericarditis.**

elim: Dissection is tearing pain to the back with BP difference.
ACS ST elevation follows one territory with reciprocal changes.
Costochondritis is reproducible on palpation with a normal ECG.
PE gives hypoxia and a sinus tachycardia, not saddle ST elevation.

steps.x: **C.** Sitting forward + rub = pericarditis.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man is brought in after a stab wound to the left chest. His pulse rate is 136 bpm, BP 72/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His neck veins are distended and heart sounds are very quiet. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally and the trachea is central.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Beck's triad (raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds) after penetrating trauma is cardiac tamponade. Equal breath sounds and a central trachea argue against tension pneumothorax.

steps.x: Diagnosis of shock with raised JVP.
Beck's triad after trauma; chest exam normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cardiac tamponade.**

elim: MI would not follow a stab wound or muffle the heart sounds.
Dissection gives tearing pain and unequal pulses.
Massive PE gives hypoxia; saturations are 96%.
Tension gives absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation.

steps.x: **C.** Beck's triad = tamponade.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer is breathless and light-headed. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 86/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Her JVP is raised to the earlobes and heart sounds are muffled. Echo shows a large pericardial effusion.
practice.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
practice.e: In cardiac tamponade, systolic BP falls by more than 15 mmHg on inspiration (pulsus paradoxus). Pulsus alternans is severe LV failure.

steps.x: Finding on examination in tamponade.
Malignant effusion with Beck's triad: tamponade.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pulsus paradoxus.**

elim: A bounding pulse is CO2 retention or high output states.
Collapsing pulse is aortic regurgitation.
Pulsus alternans is severe LV systolic failure.
Slow-rising pulse is aortic stenosis.

steps.x: **D.** Tamponade = pulsus paradoxus (>15 mmHg).

practice.stem: A 58 year old man had cardiac surgery 3 years ago. He has 8 months of increasing ankle swelling, abdominal distension and fatigue. His pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 112/74 mmHg. His JVP is raised, there is a positive hepatojugular reflux, ascites and an early diastolic extra sound. Lateral chest X-ray shows pericardial calcification.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Slowly progressive right heart failure signs with a pericardial knock and pericardial calcification after cardiac surgery is constrictive pericarditis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of chronic right heart failure signs.
Chronic, knock, calcified pericardium, raised JVP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Constrictive pericarditis.**

elim: Tamponade is acute with hypotension.
DCM gives a displaced apex, S3 and pulmonary oedema, not a knock.
Cirrhosis does not raise the JVP.
Nephrotic syndrome gives proteinuria and a normal JVP.

steps.x: **B.** Raised JVP + knock + calcified pericardium = constriction.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man had an anterior myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago. He now has fever, malaise and sharp chest pain that is worse on inspiration and eased sitting forward. A friction rub is heard. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pericarditis with fever weeks after MI is Dressler's syndrome, an autoimmune pericarditis. Papillary rupture is 2–10 days and gives a new murmur.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a post-MI complication.
Weeks after MI + pericarditic pain + rub + fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dressler's syndrome.**

elim: An LV aneurysm gives persistent ST elevation and heart failure, not a rub with fever.
Papillary rupture is 2–10 days with acute MR.
PE gives hypoxia and no rub.
Free wall rupture is sudden tamponade within days.

steps.x: **A.** Weeks after MI + pericarditis = Dressler's.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has 4 months of fatigue, joint pains, mouth ulcers and a rash over her cheeks that is worse in the sun. She now has breathlessness and quiet heart sounds. Echo shows a moderate pericardial effusion. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her effusion?
practice.e: Arthralgia, oral ulcers, a photosensitive malar rash and serositis in a young woman is SLE, a recognised risk factor for pericardial effusion and tamponade.

steps.x: Cause of a pericardial effusion: read the background.

clues: rash over her cheeks that is worse in the sun
steps.x: Young woman with malar rash, oral ulcers, arthralgia: lupus serositis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Hypothyroid effusions come with weight gain and cold intolerance.
RA gives symmetrical small-joint synovitis but not a malar rash or oral ulcers.
Sarcoid gives hilar nodes and lupus pernio (not lupus).
TB gives sweats, weight loss and cough.

steps.x: **D.** Malar rash + ulcers + serositis = SLE.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has acute pericarditis after a viral illness. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. His 12-lead ECG shows several abnormalities.
practice.q: Which ECG finding is most specific for acute pericarditis?
practice.e: PR depression is the most specific ECG finding of acute pericarditis. Saddle ST elevation is common but less specific.

steps.x: The question asks for the MOST SPECIFIC finding, not the most common.
Pericarditis ECG: saddle ST elevation, PR depression, Spodick's sign.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **PR depression.**

elim: Electrical alternans is a large effusion.
Q waves suggest established infarction.
Saddle ST elevation is common but less specific (early repolarisation looks similar).
T inversion appears late and is non-specific.

steps.x: **B.** Most specific = PR depression.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman on apixaban becomes breathless and dizzy. Her pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 84/58 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her JVP is raised and heart sounds are quiet. The ECG shows small QRS complexes that alternate in height.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Echocardiography is the gold standard for pericardial effusion and tamponade, showing fluid and right heart diastolic collapse at the bedside.

steps.x: Confirm suspected tamponade.
Anticoagulated, Beck's triad, electrical alternans: haemopericardium with tamponade.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bedside echocardiography.**

elim: MRI is slow and unsafe in a shocked patient.
CXR may show a water bottle heart but cannot confirm tamponade.
CTPA is for PE and delays treatment.
Troponin does not show fluid.

steps.x: **E. Echo** confirms tamponade.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man has acute viral pericarditis. He has no past medical history and takes no medications. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. Echo shows no effusion.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: First-line treatment for acute pericarditis is an NSAID plus colchicine with rest. Colchicine alone is for those who cannot take NSAIDs.

steps.x: Initial management of uncomplicated pericarditis.
No contraindication to NSAIDs; nothing to drain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **NSAID + colchicine.**

elim: Dual antiplatelets are for ACS.
Colchicine alone is second-line (e.g. peptic ulcer).
Steroids are not first-line and raise recurrence.
There is no effusion to drain.

steps.x: **C. Ibuprofen + colchicine.**

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has acute pericarditis. She had a bleeding duodenal ulcer 2 months ago and is still taking omeprazole. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. Echo shows a trivial effusion.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: NSAIDs should be avoided in peptic ulcer disease, so colchicine monotherapy is the second-line option.

steps.x: Management: check for a reason to avoid NSAIDs.
Recent bleeding peptic ulcer: no NSAID.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Colchicine monotherapy.**

elim: Antiplatelets would risk more bleeding and are for ACS.
Ibuprofen is an NSAID.
Naproxen is an NSAID.
A trivial effusion is just monitored.

steps.x: **B.** Peptic ulcer = colchicine alone.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man is 5 days after a permanent pacemaker insertion. He becomes confused and breathless. His pulse rate is 138 bpm, BP 78/52 mmHg, and systolic BP falls 20 mmHg on inspiration. His JVP is raised and heart sounds are muffled. Bedside echo shows a large effusion with right ventricular collapse.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Cardiac tamponade needs urgent pericardiocentesis, preferably sub-xiphoid under ultrasound. Diuretics and nitrates reduce preload and worsen shock.

steps.x: Initial management of tamponade.
Post-procedure tamponade with pulsus paradoxus and echo confirmation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent pericardiocentesis.**

elim: Furosemide reduces preload and worsens tamponade.
GTN lowers preload and BP further.
Pericardiectomy is for constrictive pericarditis.
Thrombolysis could worsen bleeding into the pericardium.

steps.x: **E.** Tamponade = drain it now.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman with lung cancer has a large pericardial effusion. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low-voltage QRS complexes whose height alternates from beat to beat.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the alternating QRS height?
o: Beat-to-beat swinging of the heart within the effusion
practice.e: Electrical alternans reflects the heart swinging within a large effusion, changing its electrical axis from beat to beat.

steps.x: Mechanism of an ECG sign.
Big effusion, low voltage, alternans.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The heart **swings** in the fluid, so the axis changes each beat.

elim: Alternating BBB changes QRS shape and width, not just height.
Hyperkalaemia gives peaked T waves and broad QRS.
Infiltration would not alternate beat to beat.
Phrenic irritation causes hiccups, not ECG change.

steps.x: **B.** Alternans = swinging heart.
